description:
Team PARAMOST:

Maksudali Imomaliyev and Shavkat Jumanov, high school students at Al-Beruniy school, Tashkent. 

Maksudali: programmer interested in low-level systems and robotics; 

Shavkat focuses on data science.

We chose Planet X and SPHEREx because it is the most challenging and teaches what we want to learn: real NASA data and astronomical image processing. 

We plan to build a public tool showing how the sky changes over time, complete the challenge and ofc aim to win.
summary: In the 1420s, Mirzo Ulugbek measured the position of about a thousand stars from his observatory in Samarkand. And his catalogue was among the most accurate of its time. But the sky does not stand still, nor does it wait. PARAMOST is a free web tool that lets anyone see that motion in NASA's newest all-sky infrared data. Type a star name or coordinates and the tool downloads SPHEREx images of that patch of sky, cleans them using SPHEREx's own quality flags, stacks each six-monthly visit, and plays them as a short video, so moving and changing objects stand out. Users can choose detectors and wavelengths, add or subtract visits, overlay Gaia and CatWISE catalogues, and measure light curves and 102-channel spectra on the fly. We tested it on all five challenge targets, including Barnard's Star and WISE 0855. Our goal is to make SPHEREx data usable without code, for students, amateurs, and scientists.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

PARAMOST turns SPHEREx's raw infrared images into something anyone can explore. A user enters an object name (e.g. "Barnard's Star") or coordinates, chooses a field of view, a detector or wavelength range, and gets:

- a video of that patch of sky across SPHEREx visits (about every six months), with an interactive player showing real dates and optional real-time gaps;

- a deep picture (all visits added) and a "later minus earlier" difference picture where a moving object appears as a red/blue pair;

- Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 catalogue overlays, moved to the date of each visit using proper motion, plus known asteroids from IMCCE SkyBoT;

- a light curve (brightness over time at one wavelength) and a 102-channel spectrum per visit, measured on the fly with aperture photometry;

- a view of SPHEREx's data-quality flags for the area;

- an Aladin Lite (CDS) viewer showing the wider sky in WISE/2MASS/DSS for context;

- shareable links: coordinates and settings are kept in the URL so that any view can be reopened or embedded.

HOW IT WORKS

The data side is a Python library (spherex/ (that was coded by our team using encouraged tools such as astropy, astroquery, and the IRSA tutorials) with one documented interface (api.py) used by a Streamlit web app.

1. Find: queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images covering the position, automatically picking up new data releases (QR2, QR3, DR1).

2. Download and cache: fetches small cutouts and keeps them on disk, so repeat views are fast and the five challenge targets work even without internet.

3. Clean: reads each image's flag mask, supporting both the older and newer SPHEREx flag formats, and removes bad pixels. Saturated star cores are handled correctly: pixels with a valid corrected value are kept, true early-overflow pixels are only filled for display and are never used for measurements.

4. Stack: groups frames into visits, reprojects them onto one grid, and combines them with a sigma-clipped mean (median or raw value when a visit has only 1-3 frames) to remove cosmic rays and single-frame defects. A raw-average option is kept, so nothing is hidden.

5. Compare: difference, sum, subtract-the-average, two-band difference and three-detector colour images.

6. Measure: aperture photometry with sky annulus, saturation and neighbour-star warnings, and a wavelength-spread warning on light curves.

RESULTS ON THE FIVE CHALLENGE TARGETS

- Barnard's Star: its proper motion (~10 arcsec/year) is visible between visits.

- WISE 0855: the faint, cold brown dwarf is recovered where its proper motion predicts, with brightness consistent with the catalogue; the tool warns that a nearby star dominates at short wavelengths.

- R Draconis and RW Aurigae: brightness changes between visits appear in the video and light curves.

- Epsilon Indi B: detected and tracked; the tool shows how measured brightness depends on exact wavelength on a steep spectrum.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

SPHEREx data normally requires knowledge of FITS files, bit masks and coordinate systems. PARAMOST makes it accessible from a browser in seconds for cached targets and in a few minutes for any new position. Students and amateur astronomers can find moving and variable objects themselves; scientists can quickly check a source before deeper analysis. It is designed to be easy to update as new SPHEREx releases arrive.

CREATIVITY

Inspired by Mirzo Ulugbek's observatory in Samarkand, which mapped the sky as it was, our tool shows how the sky changes, turning a static infrared survey into time-lapse video and spectra anyone can explore.

We had our pipeline independently reviewed against real cached data several times and fixed every issue found, including flag-format differences between releases, saturation handling and catalogue epochs. The tool shows warnings instead of presenting saturated, contaminated or few-frame results as discoveries.

Python, astropy, astroquery, photutils, reproject, NumPy, Matplotlib, Streamlit, HTML/JavaScript (video player), Aladin Lite, Git/GitHub, DigitalOcean (Ubuntu, nginx, systemd).

USE OF AI TOOLS
We used AI assistants (Claude, and OpenCode) to help write and review parts of the Python code, to draft documentation and function descriptions, and to help draft this submission text. All scientific decisions, testing on real SPHEREx data and final code were checked by our team. No images, video or audio were AI-generated.
